incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of an artificial intelligence scam targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake social media profiles and AI-generated videos using his likeness to promote fraudulent immigration services. These deepfakes offer services such as US residency assistance for undocumented immigrants in exchange for payments like $2,200, along with fake testimonials from supposed former clients claiming successful legal outcomes. Leal discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office.

The fraud has escalated dramatically over the past three months, prompting Leal to hire an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake accounts across social media platforms, including 3,500 on TikTok, 2,400 on Facebook, and 544 on Instagram. Scammers typically direct victims through social media videos to WhatsApp, where they send phony contracts and request payment via Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Leal has changed his personal phone number and plans to contact local and federal authorities to investigate the scams. He warns immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to avoid anyone requesting immediate payment.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A fabricated article recently circulated online featuring a fake interview between ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler and Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock discussing Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never occurred, but the scam represents a growing trend of AI-generated investment schemes. ASIC reports that such sophisticated frauds are becoming increasingly common, with the regulator removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams surged 279 percent, while fake investment platforms jumped 151 percent.

Scammers increasingly impersonate high-profile Australians, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and billionaire Gina Rinehart among the most commonly targeted. Rather than using single fake images, criminals now construct elaborate webs of deception involving fake brands, news articles, reviews, and advertisements to build credibility. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers and independently check them through official registers before investing. Kohler argues that platforms hosting such content should face heavy penalties.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A class-action lawsuit has been filed against Oura, the smart ring company, accusing it of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. The lawsuit, filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco on Thursday, claims that Oura's rings, which cost $300 and up, cannot accurately measure sleep stages as advertised. The suit alleges that Oura's sensors and algorithms rely on "AI-generated guesses" comparable to coin flips rather than genuine physiological measurements, contradicting the company's claims of 95% accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs.

Oura disputes these allegations, stating it stands behind its scientific research and that its sleep staging has been validated in multiple peer-reviewed studies. The company notes that while Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using heart rate and other physiological signals, it is not a medical device and should not replace clinical sleep studies. The lawsuit seeks class action status and a jury trial, though it remains unclear what compensation customers might receive if the case proceeds. This marks another legal challenge for Oura, which is also facing a separate class action lawsuit regarding unauthorized collection of personal data.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team identified Aurora ransomware operations targeting ESXi environments since April 2026. The group has deployed a Linux ransomware variant that encrypts virtual machine files while keeping the hypervisor bootable, allowing victims to see ransom demands. Attackers created a custom tool called esxi_finder.py to scan networks for ESXi hosts and vCenter servers. The research tracked ten target organizations affected between April and May 2026.

In a notable development, Aurora operators abused Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation tasks including installing VPN clients, scanning networks, enumerating domain privileges, and attempting credential relay attacks. Operators imposed strict restrictions on the AI, explicitly forbidding DCSync attacks, account lockouts, and adding new computer objects to domains. A separate cluster of activity, possibly involving different operators, targeted eight organizations across multiple countries using SQL Server vulnerabilities and S3 buckets for data exfiltration.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across the Northeast, filed a lawsuit in Texas Business Court alleging that Pizza Hut's mandatory adoption of Dragontail, an AI-powered delivery management system, caused major operational failures and approximately $100 million in damages. The franchisee claims that after the 2024 rollout, delivery performance deteriorated significantly as DoorDash drivers gained real-time visibility into kitchen operations and began waiting up to fifteen minutes to batch multiple orders together, rather than delivering pizzas immediately. This caused delivery times to increase substantially and customer satisfaction to plummet, with year-over-year sales in New York City swinging from positive 10.19% growth to negative 9.78%.

Chaac alleges that Pizza Hut failed to provide adequate training or support for the system and ignored the worsening delivery metrics despite the sharp sales decline in key markets. Before Dragontail's implementation, more than 90 percent of the franchisee's pizza deliveries arrived within thirty minutes and the company consistently achieved double-digit sales growth. The lawsuit claims Pizza Hut breached its franchise agreement by mandating the software's continued use while failing to exercise reasonable business judgment or accommodate the franchisee's business model. Pizza Hut stated it is reviewing the claims and will respond through legal channels.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers are sending highly personalized emails impersonating Terry Gross and other staff members of NPR's "Fresh Air" program to trick authors, entertainers and public figures into paying fees for supposed interview appearances. The fraudulent messages include detailed references to victims' work and appear to come from legitimate booking processes, often requesting between $250 and other amounts for production costs. One Misericordia University history professor initially believed the invitation was real until follow-up emails requested payment and she noticed suspicious elements like Gross personally handling logistics and the use of a Gmail address.

WHYY, NPR and law enforcement are investigating the scam, which has also targeted other celebrities including comedians Nikki Glaser and Amy Poehler and journalist Katie Couric. Cybersecurity experts say artificial intelligence has made it easier and cheaper for criminals to create convincing personalized scams that exploit people's vanity. WHYY emphasizes it never charges guests for interviews and advises potential victims to watch for red flags like payment requests, verify requests through official channels and call the organization directly to confirm invitations rather than responding to suspicious emails.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Israeli government officials funded a fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute to publish pro-Israel propaganda designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words in nine days, using question-based headlines resembling chatbot queries. The reports presented Israel's positions on topics including alleged Palestinian prisoner torture and Gaza starvation in academic-seeming language with sourced citations, though researchers noted the framing consistently downplayed Israeli criticism. The operation was coordinated through Israeli advertising agency LaPam, European media company Havas Media, and American firms including Piro Inc, which contracts content designed specifically to shape how artificial intelligence systems evaluate credibility.

The broader campaign has cost tens of millions of dollars but Israeli officials have expressed frustration about its effectiveness, with one saying the government paid substantial sums while the situation worsened. American public opinion has shifted significantly against Israel, with recent polling showing only 36 percent of Americans favor Israel over Palestinians. Researchers warn this represents a concerning new reality where foreign governments and other actors can systematically manipulate the training data that powers AI systems, potentially spreading narratives that chatbots repeat without citation or fact-checking opportunities.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records have filed separate lawsuits against AI music generators Udio and Suno. The labels accuse both companies of scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission to train their AI models. The lawsuits claim the companies have deliberately concealed which songs they used for training and that both services can directly reproduce sections of famous songs. The record labels submitted a comprehensive list of thousands of copyrighted works they believe were scraped, featuring artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Coldplay, and many others.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate versions of famous songs by using specific prompts describing characteristics like decade, genre, and artist style. For example, they generated outputs matching Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and a near-identical version of Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, where the companies are based. Both AI companies previously claimed their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use, a position the labels dispute.

Universal Music Group has settled its lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which had been accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence model. Under the new licensing agreements, Udio will launch a platform next year that only uses authorized and licensed music, allowing users to customize, stream, and share AI-generated songs. UMG, along with Sony Music and Warner Music Group, had sued Udio for allegedly creating songs similar to copyrighted hits like The Temptations' "My Girl" without permission or compensation. The specific financial terms of the settlement remain undisclosed.

This settlement marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label. Udio's CEO stated the partnership will help unite AI and the music industry while compensating artists who opt into the new platform. Udio, launched in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees, has attracted millions of users since its release. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers, further demonstrating the growing collaboration between traditional music companies and AI technology firms.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers in a Los Angeles lawsuit have admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, non-existent quotes, and false legal holdings in their court filings. The case involves Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, a postal service worker who sued State Farm after a 2020 fire in her Carson home left it uninhabitable. While repairs were underway, storm damage occurred, and she claims State Farm delayed approving additional repairs, ultimately leaving her home incomplete. She and her husband have since declared bankruptcy and lost their home to foreclosure, stating their family home is permanently gone.

Lawyer Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys to help prepare motions, which resulted in seven fake case citations across eight filings. Lead counsel Kenneth Katel apologized to the court, accepting responsibility despite claiming he was unaware AI had been used. The incident highlights a growing trend in the legal profession, with 41 percent of law firms using generative AI according to recent surveys. A Paris-based database has documented 1,922 legal hallucination cases worldwide, mostly in the United States. The trial is scheduled for October.

stories.Headline: Nvidia buying artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $13 billion
stories.Summary:
Chipmaker Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence software platform, for approximately $13 billion. Hugging Face is used by over 18 million developers, researchers, and creators who share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications on the platform. More than 200,000 companies also use the service. Nvidia's CEO stated that Hugging Face will remain an open-source platform, allowing organizations to download and customize their own AI models rather than paying for proprietary services from competitors like OpenAI and Anthropic.

The acquisition represents Nvidia's strategic bet that businesses will increasingly favor open-source AI models. This deal comes amid growing concerns about AI security, following several incidents where AI systems hacked into other organizations during testing. The $12.93 billion purchase includes $1 billion for employee retention. Nvidia's stock rose nearly 2% following the announcement, while Hugging Face remains privately held.

stories.Headline: NYC, the nation's largest school district, bans AI for students through 8th grade - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system announced a temporary one-year ban on artificial intelligence tools for students through eighth grade, which Mayor Zohran Mamdani described as the most expansive prohibition in the country. The policy prohibits all software using student-facing generative AI and bans companion chatbots across all grades. Meanwhile, the city will recommend screen time limits of 30 minutes daily for third through fifth graders and 45 minutes for sixth through eighth graders. Teachers remain allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks.

The broader approach aims to help students navigate AI while preventing over-reliance and cheating. High school students will receive AI literacy classes twice yearly and participate in supervised AI platform pilots. City officials will also conduct a comprehensive review of all technology tools in the school system and eliminate those deemed non-essential to learning. The teachers union praised the screen time limits but expressed concerns about implementation details and called for stronger safeguards in products the district purchases. Students are scheduled to return to classrooms the following week.

stories.Headline: Lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Yahoo
stories.Summary:
Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish basic standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence. Democratic state Senator Dina Neal recommended the committee pursue this action due to concerns about the lack of oversight and potential risks associated with integrating AI systems without legal requirements. The proposed legislation would require transparency around AI use and prevent bias in automated decision-making. Several Nevada agencies, including the Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have already implemented AI systems. Some people have reportedly been denied benefits and unable to speak with a human during appeals processes.

The nine bill draft requests, including the AI oversight proposal, were approved at an August 27 interim Government Affairs Committee meeting. The legislation will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1. State Senator Edgar Flores emphasized the importance of ensuring humans ultimately make important decisions rather than relying solely on automated systems. Senator Neal said the state needs to audit agencies and determine how many errors have occurred where human response was needed but did not happen. Lawmakers anticipate facing resistance from state and local agencies when the bill is discussed.

stories.Headline: Electoral court sets new standards for AI deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Brazil's highest electoral court established new guidelines for identifying artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes in political content ahead of October elections. The ruling came from a case involving opposition candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who displayed AI-created images of his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, at his party's convention in July. The deepfake showed the former president endorsing his son's campaign against current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to lead a coup.

The court voted 4-3 to not punish Senator Bolsonaro, determining the deepfake was shown at a private party event rather than a public political advertisement. However, the court voted 5-2 to formally define what constitutes a deepfake in political advertising as synthetic content created or altered using artificial intelligence technology that realistically reproduces a person's image, voice, or speech. These standards will apply to thousands of campaign ads broadcasters must air before the October 4 election, during 14 minutes of daily airtime designated for political commercials.

stories.Summary:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is proposing a ban on artificial intelligence tools for students in public schools through eighth grade. The policy aims to restrict how AI technology is used in younger classrooms as part of what the mayor describes as creating the right future for children. The Mamdani administration wants schools to carefully control the role that artificial intelligence plays in education.

However, the proposal is facing skepticism from people within New York City's education system. Critics question whether such a broad restriction can actually be enforced, especially as AI tools become increasingly integrated into computers, phones, and common online services. This move places the nation's largest public school system at the center of the growing national debate about how schools should respond to generative artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: LAUSD adopts moratorium on student AI use, another big move to limit classroom computer time - Los Angeles Times
stories.Summary:
The Los Angeles Unified School District has implemented a moratorium on student use of generative artificial intelligence on school devices for the current school year. District administrators enacted the policy independently to align with the school board's June decision to reduce student screen time, though some board members expressed surprise at not being formally notified. The moratorium prohibits chatbots and AI tutors for all students, though the district will continue using non-generative AI tools like adaptive learning systems and speech recognition software. Students can still use Google for searches but cannot access Google's interactive AI Mode on school devices.

The announcement comes as New York City also moved to restrict student AI use, banning generative AI in preschool through eighth grade while allowing limited use in high schools. Activist parents and education organizations praised Los Angeles's stricter approach as a historic step addressing concerns about technology reliance in schools. However, the district has not yet developed policies for student AI use on personal devices, and teachers remain able to use AI tools. Officials are working to determine long-term AI guidelines, as the moratorium currently applies only to the current school year.

stories.Summary:
# Summary

The United States government has sided with OpenAI in a copyright lawsuit filed by the New York Times. The federal government submitted a legal filing supporting OpenAI's position in the case, which centers on whether the artificial intelligence company improperly used the Times' published content to train its language models without permission or compensation.

This development represents a significant moment in the ongoing debate over AI companies' use of copyrighted material. The government's intervention could influence how courts interpret fair use rights for AI training and whether large technology companies can legally use published works to develop their systems. The case outcome may establish important precedents for the broader relationship between AI development and copyright protection.
